headline: Approved April 23, 2026 minutes as amended, and reviewed CDBG program status and Economic Development Action Plan matrix.
summary: The Council approved the April 23, 2026 meeting minutes as amended. Members heard a CDBG update on the housing rehab program, a presentation from Mayor Cahill on City finances and the trash fee, and discussed the Economic Development Action Plan matrix and possible partnerships.
decisions: Approved the April 23, 2026 meeting minutes, as amended, by a vote of 11-0.

2. CDBG Update – Darlene Wynne 29 
 30 
Wynne explained that the Community Development Manager was hired in February and has 31 
been working on getting the pre-grant startup requirements completed, including a full 32 
environmental review. This project is a housing rehab program that does not yet have sites 33 
defined and so it is difficult to know if they are historic sites. The sites will need to be assessed 34 
as to whether they are subject to floodplain, historic, or other regulations. The City had a 30 day 35 
notice prior to a request for the funds to be released and this has been signed off on. The City is 36 
contracting with its vendor, Habitat for Humanity, with a kickoff meeting yesterday. The funding 37 
for the project is supposed to be spent in 18 months. The City was notified that is was awarded 38 
the grant on October 22nd but could not say anything about it until mid-December when the State 39 
announced it. Work did not truly begin until January. The City can  request an extension once a 40 
better timeline for the project is known. In the meantime, the City successfully applied for the 41 
next round of funding which starts July 1st. Notice of the award will not likely happen until 42 
September. The applicant includes new programs such as a small business micro enterprise loan 43 
program, housing rehab, and two public social services.  44

3. Mayor Michael P. Cahill conversation 46 
 47 
Mayor Cahill noted that the Council took the first of two necessary votes to raise the trash fee. 48 
The Council is raising it to a lower number than what he requested but this will cover a good 49 
amount of the trash and recycling costs, though still leaving the City with a balance to cover. 50 
Cities and towns all over the region are making significant cuts. Large State aid cuts were made 51 
over the two recessions of 2003 and 2008. The State cut over $7,000,000 in aid to Beverly and 52 
the City has never really recovered. State aid used to make up 24% of the City’s budget and now 53 
makes up about 13% of the budget. This is definitely impacting how the City is able to do its 54 
business. The combination of raising property taxes to the max and whatever State aid is sent, is 55 
just not enough. One big revenue source is auto taxes, but people continue to buy fewer cars. 56 
Another big piece is new growth. Any investment made in properties creates new value, which 57 
gets captured during assessments. This is part of the reason that there is interest in spending 58 
energy on an Economic Development Action Plan. There is interest in raising new growth to 59 
help meet the budgetary needs. There is also interest in the overall wellness of the community. 60 
The City is mandated by the State to raise pension investments by approximately 4.5% per year. 61 
This year, that is almost $700,000 more than last year. The City is on target to fully fund its 62 
pension system in 2032. At that point, the City will be approximately $18M per year into its 63 
pensions and some of that money will become available for other purposes. There is another 64 
large liability of approximately $300M in post-employment benefits. There are some cost 65 
increases every year that are well above 2.5%. The City will be putting in for a 9% premium 66 
increase for healthcare, of which the City pays 80% and employees pay 20%.  67 
 68 
Mayor Cahill stated that, aside from taking care of the assets, infrastructure, etc., the other big 69 
thing that cities do is to deliver services, and this costs money. The City has been trying to put as 70 
much as possible into the schools, increasing school spending by $5.6M two years ago, $7.6M 71 
last year, and $4.5M this year. Thus, while there was some upheaval over the increased trash fee, 72 
and it is impactful to raise a fee by a significant amount in the middle of all the affordability 73 
challenges people are facing., he believes this will level out fairly quickly.  74 
 75 
Mayor Cahill stated that the City’s affordability questions are not going to get easier going into 76 
next year because the secondary sewage treatment plant is 30 years old and much of the 77 
equipment has reached an end of life cycle. Thus, there is an $800M capital plan that needs to be 78 
carried out for the next 15-20 years. The customers collectively have to pay for all the 79 
improvements through water and sewer rate increases. The water treatment district is about two 80 
years behind the sewerage district in coming to cities and towns looking for more money. 81 
Beverly's average property tax bill is modest in the context of the county. The City’s average 82 
property tax bill is 14th in the county, meaning that 13 communities have a lower average bill and 83 
21 communities have a higher average bill. The City has worked hard to keep the water and 84 
sewer rates from ballooning up, while increasing them to cover needs. The community is doing a 85 
good job of keeping the tax burden down.  86
